Types of Targets
• As we’ve discussed, setting growth targets requires two things:
1. An achievement goal (e.g., proficiency/meeting expectations)
2. A time-frame to reach that goal (e.g., 5 years)
• In the beginning (2005 to 2008) states geared everything toward
proficiency.
• Since 2010, states have considered achievement goals besides proficiency.
• More recently, states have also begun tailoring the time frame to reach
the goal issues such as number of years student has been receiving ELL
services or the student’s proximity to the achievement goal.

Catch-Up/Keep-Up
• The most prevalent type of growth target is the Catch-Up/Keep-Up
Target
• Catch-Up: Students who are not currently meeting
expectations (level 1 or level 2) are given a trajectory to reach
proficient/meeting expectations status over a given time frame
(e.g., 5 years)
• Keep-Up: Students who are currently meeting expectations
(level 3 or level 4) are given a trajectory to maintain proficient/
meeting expectations status over a given time frame (e.g., 5
years)

Catch-Up
• The Catch-Up Target for the student is the MINIMUM of the 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 year SGP
trajectories.
• That is, the target is the ONE trajectory that catches the student up over the next 5 years.
• Most often, the least is the 5 year target, but not necessarily
• In some states the achievement levels are set unevenly in terms of difficulty so more time
doesn’t necessarily mean less difficulty to reach.
• In the example given, the 4 and 5 year trajectories are of equal difficulty.
• For each dot on each trajectory there is an associated scaled score (theta value) associated with
it.
• Though the trajectories appear straight, in reality they are usually slightly concave down
indicating larger scaled score gains in the initial years of the trajectory.
• If Grade 8 is the terminal grade, then grade 3 is the only grade with a 5 year catch-up trajectory.

Keep-Up
• The Keep-Up Target for the student is the MAXIMUM of the 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 year SGP
trajectories (40 in this case).
• That is, the target ensures that the student keeps-up for ALL of the next 5 years.
• The number of years associated maximum SGP trajectory can vary depending on a number
of factors including the normative difficulty of the achievement levels going forward
• In the example given, the 4 and 5 year trajectories are of equal difficulty.
• For each dot on each trajectory there is an associated scaled score (theta value) associated
with it.
• Though the trajectories appear straight, in reality they are usually slightly concave up.
• If Grade 8 is the terminal grade, then grade 3 is the only grade with a 5 year Keep-up
trajectory.

Move-Up/Stay-Up
• The second most prevalent type of growth target is the Move-
Up/Stay-Up Target
• Move-Up: Students who are currently meeting expectations
(level 3) but not exceeding (level 4) are given a trajectory to
reach exceeding status over a given time frame (e.g., 5 years)
• Stay-Up: Students who are currently exceeding expectations
(level 4) are given a trajectory to maintain proficient status
over a given time frame (e.g., 5 years)

WIDA-ACCESS
• WIDA-ACCESS targets are ALL catch-up targets where the
desired achievement outcome is ELP proficiency (WIDA level
• WIDA-ACCESS targets have a individual specific time-frame to
reach ELP proficiency based upon the number of years that
the student has been receiving ELL services ranging from 6
years (no services) to 1 year (5 or more years receiving
services)

Summary
• The goal of the growth-to-standard analyses is to
communicate to stakeholders a “pathway” to a desirable
achievement outcome over a given span of time.
• As the catch-up/keep-up and move-up/stay-up illustrations
show, there are consistent rules to how these interim annual
targets are set.
• As the WIDA-ACCESS illustration shows, customization can
occur by specifying a student specific time-frame.
